purpose: Primary and strong-secondary sources for lawsuits, judgments, testimony, family actions, victim-rights disputes, platform-harm evidence, witness intimidation, litigation funding, bankruptcy/settlement mechanisms, classifier defamation disputes and institutional accountability. Inclusion supports only the bounded claims listed for each source.
epistemic_rules: A complaint or allegation is not a finding.
A motion-to-dismiss ruling generally tests legal sufficiency while accepting well-pleaded allegations as true; it does not establish the allegations as fact.
A settlement resolves claims but ordinarily does not establish liability unless the settlement or judgment says otherwise.
A judgment, conviction, official inquiry finding or coroner finding may support stronger status labels within its exact scope.
A death must never be causally attributed to a person, forum, platform or campaign unless a coroner, court, medical authority or other competent official source makes that causal finding.
Family testimony and survivor testimony are first-person evidence and should be preserved as testimony, not silently upgraded into adjudicated fact.
Private relatives and survivors should be anonymized unless their public identity is necessary to understand a public record and they have already been publicly identified.
Defamation judgments and classifier lawsuits require exact procedural status because dismissal, summary judgment, default judgment, settlement and trial verdict mean different things.

sources.publisher: Courts and Tribunals Judiciary / HM Coroner
sources.title: Molly Russell: Prevention of Future Deaths report
supports: The inquest conclusion stated that Molly Russell died from an act of self-harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content.
The coroner found it likely that viewed material affected her mental health negatively and contributed to her death in a more than minimal way.
The report identified concerns including age separation, age verification, age-specific content, algorithms, advertising and parental access/control.
sources.limitation: This supports the specific coroner findings in this case; it does not justify causal claims about unrelated deaths or platforms.

sources.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit via Justia
sources.title: Estate of Bride v. Yolo Technologies, Inc.
supports: The court described severe harassment through the YOLO anonymous-messaging app and Carson Bride's death by suicide.

The Ninth Circuit held that Section 230 barred product-liability theories tied to publication of third-party content but did not bar misrepresentation claims based on YOLO's own promise to unmask or ban abusive users.
The opinion records the family's repeated attempts to contact the service after Carson's death.
sources.limitation: The appellate ruling addresses pleading and Section 230 boundaries; it does not adjudicate every factual allegation or establish YOLO as the cause of the death.

sources.publisher: Cloudflare
sources.title: Blocking Kiwifarms
supports: Cloudflare terminated security services for Kiwi Farms after describing an escalating emergency and specific targeted threats.
Cloudflare characterized the action as extraordinary and tied it to an immediate threat to human life.
sources.limitation: A service provider's risk decision is not a judicial finding and does not prove causal responsibility for any death.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Utah via Justia
sources.title: Greer v. Moon et al., Document 453
supports: The current Greer v. Moon/Lolcow LLC case is principally a copyright-infringement action.
The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the first amended complaint.
The court record identifies Lolcow LLC as doing business as Kiwi Farms and Joshua Moon as its sole member.
sources.limitation: Earlier Greer tort/defamation theories and later copyright claims must not be conflated; denial of a motion to dismiss is not a merits finding.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Utah via Justia
sources.title: Greer v. Moon et al., Document 361 / related orders
supports: The same litigation also produced sanctions and discovery disputes against the plaintiff.
The record therefore provides counterevidence against treating the existence of litigation itself as validation of every allegation.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York
sources.title: Chicago Man Pleads Guilty to Stalking R. Kelly Victim
supports: Donnell Russell, described as Kelly's self-described manager/advisor/friend, pleaded guilty to stalking a Kelly victim.
DOJ said Russell harassed and intimidated the victim and her mother after the victim filed a civil lawsuit and while she was a likely witness.
Threats included disclosure of sexually explicit photographs and sexual history if the victim did not withdraw her lawsuit and cease participation in a negative campaign.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice
sources.title: Justice Department Reaches Civil Settlement with Victims Abused by Lawrence Nassar
supports: DOJ settled 139 administrative claims alleging inadequate FBI investigation for a total of $138.7 million.
DOJ referenced the 2021 Inspector General report critical of aspects of the FBI response and investigation.
sources.limitation: The settlement resolves claims and does not erase the OIG's explicit finding that it did not find evidence the failures were motivated by intent to interfere.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary
sources.title: Dereliction of Duty: Examining the Inspector General's Report on the FBI's Handling of the Larry Nassar Investigation
supports: The Senate hearing took testimony from Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney, Maggie Nichols and Aly Raisman.
It also took testimony from DOJ Inspector General Michael Horowitz and FBI Director Christopher Wray.
sources.limitation: Witness testimony should remain attributed to the witness unless independently corroborated or adopted in an official finding.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice
sources.title: Statement on DOJ Office of Professional Responsibility Report on Jeffrey Epstein 2006-2008 Investigation
supports: DOJ OPR did not find professional misconduct by Department attorneys.
OPR concluded victims were not treated with the forthrightness and sensitivity expected by DOJ.

OPR concluded Alexander Acosta exercised poor judgment in resolving the federal investigation through the non-prosecution agreement and in failing to ensure victim notification regarding the state plea hearing.

sources.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit via Justia
sources.title: In re Courtney Wild
supports: The en banc majority held that the Crime Victims' Rights Act does not create a freestanding private action outside a preexisting criminal proceeding.
The litigation record recounts the secret non-prosecution agreement and the district court's earlier 2019 finding that victims' rights were violated.
The opinions reveal a major legal gap between acknowledged victim-treatment failures and available judicial remedies.
sources.limitation: Distinguish the en banc majority holding from dissenting judges' characterizations of the prosecutors' conduct.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York via Justia
sources.title: Doe 1 v. JP Morgan Chase & Co., Order and Final Judgment
supports: The court approved a class settlement covering people harmed, injured, exploited or abused by Epstein or persons connected with an Epstein sex-trafficking venture in the defined period.
Related court records identify the settlement amount as $290 million.
sources.limitation: Settlement approval does not itself establish every allegation against the bank.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York via Justia
sources.title: Doe 1 v. Deutsche Bank AG, Order and Final Judgment
supports: The court gave final approval to the Deutsche Bank Epstein-survivor class settlement.
Public filings and reporting identify the settlement amount as $75 million.
sources.limitation: Settlement approval is not a criminal adjudication or finding that every pleaded allegation was proven.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York via Justia
sources.title: Doe v. Bank of America, N.A., Order and Final Judgment
supports: The court entered final judgment approving a $72.5 million class settlement.
The settlement class concerns women sexually abused or trafficked by Epstein or connected persons as defined in the order.
sources.limitation: The settlement resolves allegations; it is not equivalent to an adjudicated liability finding.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York via Justia
sources.title: Doe 1 v. JP Morgan Chase & Co. / JPMorgan v. James Staley, Opinion and Order
supports: JPMorgan brought third-party claims against former executive James Staley arising from Epstein-related litigation.
The court denied Staley's motion to dismiss the third-party complaint.
sources.limitation: Denial of a motion to dismiss is not a final merits determination.

sources.publisher: Office of the New York Attorney General
sources.title: Attorney General James Helps Secure $19 Million for Sexual Misconduct and Workplace Harassment Survivors of Harvey Weinstein
supports: A proposed global settlement created an approximately $18.875 million victims' compensation fund.
The agreement released women from specified confidentiality, non-disclosure and non-disparagement clauses related to Weinstein sexual misconduct.
The OAG linked the matter to bankruptcy and class-action resolution.
sources.limitation: The press release mixes adjudicated history with the Attorney General's allegations about company conduct; preserve those statuses separately.

sources.publisher: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York
sources.title: Gawker Media Rule 2004 discovery opinion
supports: The court record states it was undisputed that Peter Thiel funded the Bollea litigation against Gawker.
The plan administrator sought discovery concerning litigation financing and potential causes of action.
The court found good cause for Thiel-related discovery subject to settlement-agreement limitations.
sources.limitation: Third-party litigation funding is lawful and the opinion did not establish that financing litigation was itself tortious; proposed conspiracy/tort theories remained hypotheses.

sources.publisher: U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of New York
sources.title: In re Giuliani opinion summarizing Freeman litigation
supports: The opinion recounts Giuliani's civil liability to Ruby Freeman and Wandrea Shaye Moss for defamation, intentional infliction of emotional distress and civil conspiracy.
A jury awarded approximately $148 million in damages, including $75 million punitive damages.
Giuliani filed bankruptcy less than a week after entry of judgment.

sources.publisher: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission / Fox Corporation
sources.title: Fox Corporation Form 8-K
supports: Fox and Dominion settled for $787.5 million.
Fox publicly acknowledged the court's rulings finding certain claims about Dominion to be false.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama via Justia
sources.title: Estate of Donald A. King et al. v. Southern Poverty Law Center, Inc.
supports: Plaintiffs challenged SPLC's classification of the Dustin Inman Society as an anti-immigrant hate group.
After discovery, the court granted SPLC summary judgment on all counts and closed the case.
The litigation demonstrates that classifier labels can themselves be litigated and judicially tested.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri via Justia
sources.title: McClanahan v. Anti-Defamation League et al.
supports: A political candidate sued ADL and Jonathan Greenblatt over an article/classification.
The court dismissed the claims with prejudice, including because the defamation complaint failed to plead actual malice adequately.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas via Justia
sources.title: Sabal v. Anti-Defamation League
supports: The court granted in part and denied in part ADL's motion to dismiss.
Some defamation and injurious-falsehood claims survived the pleading stage while a claim tied to Congressional testimony was dismissed.
sources.limitation: Survival at the pleading stage is not a finding that the challenged statements were false or defamatory.

sources.publisher: Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General
sources.title: First-term report summarizing statewide grand jury clergy-abuse investigation and reforms
supports: The statewide grand jury investigation identified 301 priests and more than 1,000 child victims in the report.
The Attorney General described extensive institutional cover-up.
Subsequent reforms strengthened mandatory reporting, clarified confidentiality-law issues and changed limitations rules.

sources.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit via Justia
sources.title: In re Boy Scouts of America and Delaware BSA LLC
supports: 82,209 unique timely abuse claims were filed by the bar date.
The bankruptcy court estimated total abuse claims at $2.4-$3.6 billion.
The plan established a settlement trust funded with approximately $2.48 billion in noncontingent assets, much of it from insurance-policy settlements.

sources.publisher: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit via Justia
sources.title: Boy Scouts of America and Delaware BSA LLC v. D.S. / J.D.
supports: The confirmed plan channels abuse claims to a settlement trust for liquidation and payment.
The 2026 appeal illustrates downstream disputes over claimant elections and payout procedures after a mass-tort bankruptcy plan is confirmed.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice / OSHA
sources.title: Justice Department and OSHA Issue Statement on Non-Disclosure Agreements That Deter Reporting of Antitrust Crimes
supports: DOJ and OSHA stated that NDAs that deter reporting of antitrust crimes undermine whistleblower protections.
They stated such NDA practices can affect charging and sentencing decisions.
